blocks.text: The fertiliser that feeds Nigerian farms starts as nitrogen from the air. The reaction that captures it never goes to completion — it stalls halfway. Engineers cannot force it further, so instead they nudge it, using a principle worked out by Le Chatelier that you can learn in one lesson.

blocks.markdown:
## Reversible reactions

Some reactions can proceed in both directions. They are written with a double arrow.

N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)

In a closed system the forward reaction starts fast and slows as reactants are used up, while the backward reaction starts at zero and speeds up as product accumulates. Eventually the two rates become equal and the reaction appears to stop.

blocks.title: Dynamic equilibrium
blocks.text: A dynamic equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction. Both reactions continue, but there is no further net change, so the concentrations of all species remain constant.

items: It is attainable only in a closed system, from which nothing escapes
The forward and backward rates are equal, not zero — the reaction has not stopped
The concentrations of reactants and products stay constant but are not necessarily equal
Observable properties such as colour and pressure become constant
It can be approached from either the reactant side or the product side and gives the same position

blocks.title: Le Chatelier's principle
blocks.text: When a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the position of equilibrium shifts in the direction that tends to oppose the change.

rows: To the right, forming more product
The system removes the added substance
Remove a product as it forms
The system replaces what was taken away
Increase pressure on a gaseous system
Towards the side with fewer gas moles
This absorbs the extra heat supplied
This releases heat to offset the cooling
Both rates increase equally, so equilibrium is only reached sooner
blocks.caption: Applying Le Chatelier's principle

blocks.title: Optimising the Haber process
blocks.prompt: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g), the forward reaction is exothermic. Deduce the conditions that give the greatest yield of ammonia, then explain why industry uses about 450 degrees Celsius rather than a low temperature.

steps.text: Count the moles of gas: 1 + 3 = 4 on the left and 2 on the right. Increasing the pressure therefore shifts the equilibrium right, towards the smaller number of gas moles, so high pressure favours ammonia.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium right and increases the yield.
On yield alone the ideal conditions would be very high pressure and a low temperature.
However, at low temperature the reaction is extremely slow, so it would take an impractically long time to reach that high yield.

Industry therefore accepts a lower equilibrium yield in exchange for a workable rate, using a compromise temperature of about 450 degrees Celsius with an iron catalyst and a pressure of roughly 200 atmospheres.
Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled, and ammonia is liquefied and removed continuously, which by Le Chatelier's principle pulls the equilibrium further to the right.

blocks.answer: High pressure and low temperature maximise the yield, but a compromise temperature of about 450 degrees Celsius with an iron catalyst is used to achieve an acceptable rate

blocks.markdown:
### The equilibrium constant

For the general reaction

aA + bB <=> cC + dD

the equilibrium constant in terms of concentration is

$K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}$

Products go on top, reactants underneath, and each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.

A large $K_c$ means the equilibrium lies well to the right and the reaction is nearly complete. A small $K_c$ means very little product forms. **$K_c$ changes only with temperature** — adding a catalyst or altering concentrations does not change its value.

blocks.title: The catalyst question
blocks.text: If asked what a catalyst does to the position of equilibrium, the answer is nothing. It speeds up the forward and backward reactions by the same factor, so equilibrium is reached sooner but with exactly the same composition.

points: A reversible reaction in a closed system reaches dynamic equilibrium when forward and backward rates are equal.
At equilibrium concentrations stay constant, but both reactions are still occurring.
Le Chatelier's principle says the system shifts to oppose any change imposed on it.
Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas; increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction.
A catalyst changes only how quickly equilibrium is reached, never its position.
Kc places products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, and depends only on temperature.
